From technology program to working system: what happens after go-live

Go-live is the start of operation, not the end of the program. How to plan support, ownership and improvement so systems keep delivering value.

4 October 2026 · Hamerkop Systems · 2 min read

Technology programs are usually planned around a go-live date. Budgets, teams and attention are focused on reaching it. Yet the period after go-live is when an institution discovers whether a new system genuinely supports its operation. Planning for that period is one of the clearest differences between programs that deliver lasting value and those that slowly fall out of use.

Plan the first weeks as a phase of their own

The first weeks after go-live, often called hypercare, need dedicated support: experts available to users, fast triage of issues, daily reviews of open items and clear communication about what has been fixed. Users who see problems resolved quickly build confidence in the system.

Define ownership before the project team leaves

  • A business owner for each major process, responsible for how it works and how it changes.
  • A system owner responsible for configuration, access and releases.
  • A support model that defines how users raise issues, how they are prioritized and who resolves them.
  • Documentation and runbooks that let the organization operate the system without relying on individuals.

Watch adoption, not just availability

A system can be fully available and still poorly used. Signs to watch include parallel spreadsheets, manual workarounds, delayed data entry and reports rebuilt outside the system. These indicate where training, process design or configuration need attention.

Review system health regularly

Periodic health reviews look at performance, data quality, open issues, security and access, integrations and upcoming changes such as regulatory updates or new business requirements. They turn support from reactive firefighting into planned maintenance.

Improve in planned cycles

Requests for change will continue after go-live. Grouping them into planned release cycles, with testing and communication, keeps the system stable while allowing it to evolve with the institution.

Discover. Design. Implement. Stabilize and improve.

The measure of success

The real test of a technology program is whether, a year after go-live, the institution relies on the system for its daily work, trusts the information it produces and can change it with confidence. That outcome is planned from the start, not left to chance.
